speechtext:
That this House call upon the Government to take immediate action to deal with drastically reduced farm incomes resulting from the 1990-91 crop year and to make required assistance available in time for spring planting to ensure viable returns for grains, oilseeds and horticultural producers.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this motion before the House today calls to the attention of the government the drastic and urgent need for emergency farm assistance this spring. It calls upon the government to provide this assistance in time for the planting season. This assistance should not only be clarified and made concrete, but should be provided to farmers in time for the planting season. We would suggest at least by the middle of next month.
It would be hard to over-emphasize the need for this assistance for the 1990-91 crop years. Clearly, I do not think anybody can remember the price of grains and oilseeds at a lower level than they are in the current crop year. Clearly, this results from a number of factors, mainly the world grain price war between the United States and the European Economic Community. Prices have been below $100 a tonne in many months of this crop year.
In fact, the chairman of the Canadian Wheat Board pointed out one sale of United States wheat subject to a subsidy program there, the export enhancement program, where the wheat was actually sold for around $70 a tonne. If you remove the transportation costs, the actual
value of the shipment dropped to something like $35 a tonne.
Clearly, this crop year has seen the lowest prices in real terms since the 1930s, perhaps ever. Those amounts of payment are clearly inadequate. As a result of this, the government's cutback and its support programs for the 1991 calendar year, total net farm incomes are projected to drop by 54 per cent.
In some provinces, Saskatchewan and Manitoba, that drops the total net farm income to below zero. There is no net farm income. Other provinces like New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island and Ontario have a very serious reduction in total net farm income, down by percentages in the upper teens. In the case of Ontario, it is around 20 per cent. Clearly, this is the most difficult year as far as cash flow that many producers have ever faced. The executive director of the Ontario Com Producers Association projected that its incomes would be lower than at any time in the 1980s. That takes in all of those extremely low years of the late 1980s.
In fact, representatives of the Ontario Com Producers told the agriculture committee just last week that farm incomes would be something below $200 million for the grains and oilseeds in the province of Ontario below what they would project or hope would be the portion provided by government if GRIP is implemented in the coming year.
The impact goes far beyond just grains and oilseeds. It affects the whole range of agriculture commodities, but especially horticulture crops. The chairman of the Ontario Fruit and Vegetable Growers' Association last week told the agriculture committee that it is in the most desperate situation that he can recall in the 35 years that he has been a fruit and vegetable producer.
He has described the need as something like $70 million of emergency or bridging assistance before some more permanent kind of program of assistance such as GRIP, the Gross Revenue Insurance Program, is put in place. He says that it is absolutely essential that that

bridging assistance be provided this spring, before the growing and the planting season.
That was the report from only one producer. It does not take into account the tremendous problems that our potato producers in Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick are facing with the virus problem there. We are told by my colleague that the need for assistance there may be of the order of $25 million.
Prairie Pools has called for assistance in the order of $1 billion in the Canadian Wheat Board area. The Third Line of Defence Committee, which the minister appointed several months ago, has been reported to say that the need is in the order of $1.2 billion as an upper figure.
The important thing to remember here is that not only are we facing a drastic world situation for grains and oilseeds prices, but we are also facing a drastic cutback in government support programs.
Figures released by the government in December show that projections for government support programs, compared with 1988, dropped by $1.8 billion.
More recent figures show a reduction in support programs, between 1989 and 1991, of $1.6 billion. We have coming together here a terrible market situation and a government policy which has reduced those support programs which are necessary if agriculture is going to survive in the current world subsidized global grain warfare which has been going on for the past five or six years.
Why the government has chosen to reduce those support programs during the last two or three years is not clear, but it certainly is causing tremendous hardship. Figures like a 54 per cent reduction in net farm income-in some provinces 100 per cent total net farm income reduction-are only cold statistics; they do not speak of the tragedy of young farmers losing their land, of family breakups, of all kinds of difficulties that are faced in the rural community. Clearly, producers who five years ago were in a very healthy or reasonably successful position are facing difficult times now.
It almost seems like the government's plan was to reduce these support programs from those that were available in 1987, 1988 and 1989 in order to create this crisis, to bring in its GRIP and NISA programs, to bring pressure on the producers. Many producers believe that
a world trade war in agriculture commodity is the responsibility of the federal government. In the United States the federal government assumes the responsibility for most its support program. In any event, whatever the game plan of the government in this regard, the resulting GRIP program that the government has proposed for the 1991-92 crop year will see the provincial governments putting up something like 60 per cent of the premiums for those programs. We have been inundated with talk of the GRIP and the NISA program across the country, but in fact GRIP-and probably NISA, with the exception of Saskatchewan-will not help out in the 1990-91 crop year. In this crop year we will see very low returns.
The crisis is now; the assistance needed is now. If farmers are to know where they are at and what their future is going to hold, they need the government to give a commitment as to the funding it is going to provide, clearly identify what basis that funding is going to be on, and make the payments before the crop season starts. The GRIP is designed for a payout in the fall of 1992. There may be interim payments later this fall and there may be interim payments next spring. We don't know about that. Clearly for the planting season, it is essential that this plan be put before the producers this spring.
When we talk about GRIP we see some provinces, like Saskatchewan, facing tremendous contributions for a province that is predominantly agriculture, with a very small non-agriculture society to pay the benefits. The question is: Can the cost to that government and to those producers be sustained over the long haul, a cost that has been estimated at something like half a billion dollars per year?
When the Minister of Finance presented his budget, he talked about $1.3 billion of assistance for agriculture. If that amount were provided immediately on a basis on which farmers would be able to calculate what assistance they were going to receive before the planting season this year, I am sure that everybody would think that was a very fair and equitable proposition.
However, the Minister of Agriculture has put out a press release stating that the $1.3 billion could be used for a number of things. It might be used for federal government premiums for the GRIP and NISA. It might be used ' for the deficit and the Canadian
March 18, 1991

Wheat Board initial payment. It might be used for the debt in the Western Grain Stabilization Fund.
All those things do not put new money into farmers' hands this spring. What farmers need is an emergency payment or pay-out, assistance now which will provide seed, fertilizer, diesel fuel, equipment repairs, help and so on, in time for the growing season this spring.
Clearly the Canadian Wheat Board account has been variously portrayed, that it will have a deficit of $750 million or a billion dollars. The federal government's share of the GRIP and NISA premiums are large amounts as well. In the Western Grain Stabilization Fund we do not know what the deficit is. We are told that it might be several hundred million dollars. If the $1.3 billion which the Minister of Finance announced in his budget is an interim payment under the western grain stabilization fund, of course that would be immediate help, provided it was made this spring.
What we are saying is that the program should be spelled out clearly, that we should not have this shell game going where there are three or four possibilities where the funds might be used, the funds mentioned in the minister's budget but not spelling out exactly how much funding is going to be made available in the current crop year in time for the planting and seeding period.
We say to the government that it should give up on that shell game. It should make it clear exactly what assistance is going to be made available. Paying off the deficit in the Western Grain Stabilization Fund or the Wheat Board account is of interest and concern to parliamentarians and to farmers, but what farmers want to know this spring is: Are they going to survive? Are they going to be able to put a crop in the ground? Are they going to get assistance on the same basis as they did in 1987, 1988 and 1989, in those years when they were facing similar deficits and similar losses of benefits from the marketplace itself.
We call on the government to provide this assistance to end the uncertainty as to whether or not there is going to be assistance, how much, and how it is going to played.

Last year the government announced some interim support. I believe it was in the order of $500 million. It called on the provincial governments to come forward and match that amount of money.
The battle raged on for two months. It was not until the end of May that there was actually some kind of an agreement. It was not until late August or some time in September when many of those payments were made, and they were relatively small payments proportionately.
Surely we do not have to go through that spectacle again this year. Surely the Minister of Agriculture can announce what the support is going to be and make it in a timely way, where it will do some good and there will not be this long game of procrastination or the long battles with the provincial governments as to whether or not they are going to match the funds, many of which would be hard put to match, especially for a province like Saskatchewan. They are already facing a premium in the new crop year of something like $160 million for GRIP. They would be hard put to match the special interim assistance that is needed for the existing crop year, 1990-1991.
We are saying that the time has come for the government to provide this assistance. It is needed now. There is no question that we have the worst situation as far as total net farm income this year, 1990, is concerned. The crisis itself has been partly created by the government drastically reducing its support programs between 1989 and 1991, the last two years. It is even lower than those previous years. It is time that provincial governments are facing the off-loading by the federal government because GRIP will require them to put up a sizeable support amount of funds to pay their share of the premiums, as will producers.
We do not think that any assistance is being provided. Many groups made the point before the agriculture committee that emergency assistance for the 1990-1991 crop year should not be coerced by signing up for GRIP.
There is going to be enough coercion because the Minister of State for Grains and Oilseeds has announced that he is not going to give the initial price until late July or toward the end of the crop year. Producers will not have the knowledge they usually have early in the spring as to what the initial price will be. There will certainly be

enough coercion there. We do not think that assistance should be tied to GRIP, as many producers have already requested and suggested.
We believe that there needs to be equal support for the horticulture industry. I mentioned earlier the requirement of Ontario fruit and vegetable producers who said that their shortfall is in the order of $70 million. The assistance required in the P.E.I. and New Brunswick areas for their difficulties has already been spelled out as well.
We think it is time that the government made a firm decision, announced it; not blame the province but just come clean and tell farmers how much the assistance will be, on what basis, and make it available in time for the planting season so it can do the most good when it is needed.

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to participate in the debate on the motion sponsored by the opposition that deals essentially with the farm income problem and calls upon the federal government to provide assistance to help the grain and oilseeds and horticultural sectors.
I must say I welcome the motion, but I question the timeliness because it comes precisely at a time when we are dealing with one of the most comprehensive income measures in 50 years. To back that up, I am going to quote some individuals who have been quoted in this place before, the five economists who have taken issue with certain parts of the GRIP and NISA proposals: Messrs. Gray, Weisensel, Rosaasen, Furtan, and Kraft. They said in a document that they presented: "The proposed GRIP and NISA programs represent the most significant Canadian agricultural legislation in the last 50 years". They indicate that it makes it the largest agricultural program ever. They go on to say that it represents a number of significant improvements over similar income support programs implemented in the past. They go on to cite that it includes payments on farm-fed grains and, second, that there is not a requirement to sell grain within a particular crop year to be eligible for a pay-out. The range of eligible crops has been expanded. The payments are more predictable and a 15 year average of prices provides more support during periods of low prices when compared to a five-year average of prices.
While they have some reservations, the over-all scope and comprehensiveness of the program is very valid and most acceptable. "GRIP", they go on to say, "has been designed to provide income support for agriculture producers across Canada in response to unprecedented low incomes in the agriculture sector".
We are dealing with it at a time when the very issue the hon. member raised is being dealt with in a very comprehensive fashion. After a series of ad hoc responses, which members on all sides of the House criticized and indeed the industry criticized, it is time now to come forth with some policy framework that provides a future for agriculture and provides some kind of an income safety net which producers can rely upon before the fact rather than after the fact.
The fact that huge amounts of money have been paid in ad hoc assistance, we still have a problem. It does speak to the requirement of having a comprehensive approach to this series of problems. That is what the farmers want and that is what industry wants. I think that is the kind of signal we must send to the international community, that we are going to continue to stand by our farmers, and that is what the safety net legislation is all about.
I am disappointed that I heard nothing new from the Liberal side. It is the same old litany and the same old rhetoric: just send money. There was nothing new. It is basically a collection of all the requests that have been made by various members in the community. There is nothing there, there is absolutely nothing there.
Let us look at the farm income picture, not to suggest for one minute that we are not going through difficulties, and put the whole thing into perspective. It is a problem that is multifaceted in nature. If we were to look at the 1980s, the last half of the 1980s showed that realized net income on average rose by 39 per cent, from an average in the first half of the 1980s of $3.1 billion realized net income to $4.2 billion realized net income. That is a 39 per cent increase in the period 1981-85 to 1985-89.
Western Canada in the last half of the 1980s experienced an 30 per cent increase over the first half, with the average realized net income rising from $1.6 billion to $2 billion. In eastern Canada there was a 47 per cent increase in realized net income in the last half of the
March 18, 1991

1980s versus the first half of the 1980s. Again, those figures were $1.5 billion versus $2.9 billion.
It is true, as the hon. member pointed out, that in 1990 we experienced a drop to around $3 billion, approximately a 25 per cent drop in realized net income. In 1991 we are projecting a further reduction. It is in anticipation of this very fact that the safety net programs were in fact designed, were brought into being and were brought before this House in a timely fashion so that we could deal with this issue not only in the short term, but indeed in the medium and long terms.
The effect of this program will reduce the shortfall by something in the order of $2.5 billion to $3 billion. It is a program designed to help producers to help themselves by providing some predictability, by providing some level of income assurance on an acreage basis, and by providing some security and stability over the long haul.
The important feature is that it has to be looked at as a package, GRIP and NISA together. The Net Income Stabilization Account will provide that long-term stability and security. I am concerned about the fact that we have become too preoccupied with one component of the program. If we go back and look at the recommendations of the task force on safety nets, we find that it was developed as a package. I hope hon. members will recognize the importance of speaking to this issue as a package, because the two are complementary to each other.
Simply put, the Gross Revenue Insurance Program is really a management tool that allows producers to use it in part of the management of their farms. It provides a shield and a safety net from the uncertainty and the disaster that have affected particularly in grains and oilseeds and that have become all too common in the past five or six years.
This government, this Prime Minister, this Minister of Finance, my predecessor, the former Minister of Agriculture, and myself have stood by farmers in the past and we are going to continue to do it in the future. There can be no doubt about that.
The bill before us is one of the most comprehensive farm income measures that has ever been introduced in the House. It is living testimony to that fact. We are going to attempt to continue, as best we can, to shield

farmers from the difficulties and misfortunes caused by circumstances beyond their control.

In terms of direct program payments in support of agriculture in the period from 1981 to 1985, let us look at the Liberal record. In the period 1981 to 1985 the average direct program payments in support of agriculture was $921 million per year. The 1986 to 1989 average was $2.7 billion, a threefold increase.
That speaks volumes about the priority, about the compassion, about the concern for the agricultural industry. That they did not need any help when they were paying 24 per cent interest rates as a result members associated with the government in 1980 to 1984 is nonsense. The problems we have in terms of debt and the level of debt is still a carryover from the good old days of 24 per cent interest rates, the 1981 to 1984 period.
In the period from 1986 to 1990 the revenue from the marketplace in agriculture accounted for only 20 per cent to 25 per cent of the realized net income. Eighty per cent of it came from governments, federal and provincial, and 80 per cent of that came from the federal government. In western Canada, particularly Saskatchewan and Manitoba, about 90 per cent of government support came from the federal government.
If we take all the support, direct and indirect programs, in 1987-88 federal and provincial support of agriculture across the country was $8.1 billion. In 1988-89 it was $7.5 billion and in 1989-90 it was $6 billion. As a matter of fact, in the last five years, 1985-86 to 1989-90, some $22.6 billion worth of federal government support was provided to agriculture and an additional $10 billion was provided by the provinces.
In the grains and oilseeds sector during that same period of time, $13.7 billion was provided in federal support. If we were to look at it another way, on per farm basis, if we take the average farmer in Saskatchewan for the period 1987-88-89, it worked out to $20,000 per farmer.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Yes, $7 wheat for a few. How much $7 could you sell in the international marketplace today? You know you couldn't.
Let us look at Quebec in 1987-88-89, the same period. On a per farm basis, the level of direct program support from the federal government works out to $14,000 per farm. What was it in 1982-83? It was $7,000 per farm. What misery, what cheapskates.
Mr. Speaker, no compassion, no care. Let them sink or swim. That was their approach.
In spite of this massive infusion of support, we still have a problem. It needs a more comprehensive approach and we need to address some of the structural problems that exist. We must spend wiser. We do have fiscal constraints, and we must adjust to some of the realities that exist. Above all, we must provide an appropriate policy framework within which farmers can plan, knowing there is a program in place, knowing there is a long-term policy in place, knowing there is a national perspective on the issue.
The multi-faceted problems we face require multifaceted solutions. The many forces at play have been recognized under the agriculture policy review process. We have to identify them and respond appropriately, and we have, through a partnership process which I think has worked very well.
We recognize there are changing market demands. We recognize there are changes in trading patterns; changes in technology; new emphasis placed on food safety; different emphasis placed on the environment; political and economic reforms occurring throughout the world; military wars. All of these things recognize the importance of agriculture in the international marketplace. Fifty per cent of our farm income is extracted from the international marketplace. We recognize that we have to make the necessary changes. It requires a timely response in an appropriate fashion.
That is why we launched the agriculture policy review and the 11 task forces that have been at work. We are now implementing a number of the recommendations. One of those is the GRIP-NISA safety net proposal. I am not going to go into detail today, because the issue is before the House and I will be appearing before a
committee this afternoon. However, I would re-emphasize the importance of this package as a program that will provide stability, predictability, bankability and some confidence for the future.
It is a national program and it is our hope that it will cover a broad range of commodities. Horticulture has been mentioned. It would be our hope that horticulture would be incorporated into this program as soon as we possibly can. There is nothing to prevent the program NISA being implemented, provided the provinces can see fit to become a party to it.
There has been a suggestion that forage should be included in 1991-92. It is very difficult to incorporate it in the transitional year, but it is our intention to ensure that it will be incorporated into the permanent program, hopefully starting in 1992-93. To the extent that we can accommodate the forage industry, either through a third line or through some add-ons that might make it appropriate for the forage industry, to ensure that there is some semblance of equity in it, we will certainly try to do that.
The potato issue is one that we are deeply concerned about. The eradication program has been outlined, in co-operation with the producers and the provincial government. We are now working on an appropriate compensation program, and that we will be in a position to announce it in due course.
I know hon. members across the way have expressed some concerns and raised some issues with regard to the legislation currently before the House. I will be in committee this afternoon. I will be addressing a number of those areas and indicating some measure of flexibility in terms of trying to accommodate some of the concerns of the members opposite.
To repeat again, this program is fundamental. It is a fundamental building block to restoring strength and vibrance to the industry. Without long-term objectives, we cannot achieve the long-term stability Canadian farmers so desperately need.
We recognize that while GRIP and NISA are good programs for the future, they will not solve all our problems. We have never suggested they would. We have suggested they were a comprehensive approach to developing a framework that would help producers manage more effectively, and provide some stability and security for the future. We also recognize that some bridging assistance will be required until the programs
March 18, 1991

produce the intended results. We have set up a third line defence committee.
The hon. member suggests we should announce our programs right now. We have been getting some criticism from the people we are consulting over the fact that we are rushing into this without giving them a full opportunity to develop options and suggestions.
We have set up a committee of some 41 people, 19 of whom are farmers. Others represent the trade, the provinces and the federal government. On March 1 and 2 in Regina, at our federal-provincial meeting, we did establish a set of principles and guidelines that would govern us in the developing of the third line of defence, (a) that the program be multi-faceted reflecting the multi-faceted nature of the problems; (b) that it be built on the objective of the new safety net program and be linked as far as possible to participation of the new safety nets; (c) that it be directed at providing a transition from income levels attained during the pre-GRIP-NISA period based on those expected with the GRIP-NISA period;
(d)	that it be tied to longer term adjustment measures;
(e)	that it be announced as soon as possible in 1991; (f) that to the greatest extent possible delivered through the GRIP-NISA delivery programs; (g) that there we should respect the need for equity among producers, commodities and the provinces; and (h) that it be funded by the federal government, conditional upon industry and provincial government commitment to address the longterm structural needs.
The committee I referred to has produced a number of options and suggestions which we are now looking at. I will be meeting with farm leaders on March 20 here in Ottawa to further flesh out some of the thoughts and ideas with respect to this.
Our objective is to tie this into the longer term program we are putting in place under GRIP and NISA and also a longer term measure of adjustment necessary to deal with some of the forces of change that are being thrust upon us. It is not a matter of just simply tiding us over until tomorrow, it is a matter of providing something that will carry us into the future. We expect that by mid-April we will be in a position to announce something concrete.

Mr. Speaker, 1990 was the year of examination and analysis; 1991 is the year for implementation and action. In addition to the launching of the safety nets, which was a priority under the agriculture policy review, we have a number of things that we must do based upon the recommendations that have been flowing from the 11 task forces. They range all the way from strengthening the management capability of our industry and improvements in long-term financing, reduction of production costs; looking at new ways to provide adjustment support when necessary-here we are looking at enhancing the Canadian rural transition program-broadening our agricultural base through diversification and value added; maximizing our trade opportunities; aggressively challenging unfair trade practices; strengthening our regions and rural communities; strengthening our processing sector; taking steps to enhance the industry's competitiveness; and freeing up the system by reforming regulations that have created barriers to competitiveness.
These approaches are all doable in a very comprehensive way because we have had that very major internal examination of our industry. We have had the kind of recommendations brought forward that are non-partisan, and are in the interests of the total industry. We are committed to that process. We are committed to acting upon those recommendations, to give real meaning to the process of the agriculture policy review.
I invited all hon. members to participate in the process, as they have. I must say that over the period of my being Minister of Agriculture I have always found them somewhat partisan but always constructive.

He started off his comments by saying that we on this side of the House were not looking for creative solutions, that we were not looking at a new policy framework and

that we were not looking for safety nets. I wanted to ask the minister a very specific question.
In 1989 the general conference of the Agricultural Institute of Canada adopted two resolutions relating to water and the free trade agreement. I am sure the minister is well aware of that institute's concerns. I was wondering what his views were in us making sure that water was, in fact, exempt from the free trade agreement and that maybe it could be used as one of these safety nets he talks about for future negotiation for the agricultural community of this country. I wonder if the minister could comment on that.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Of course, I will comment on it. I do not know what the hon. member is fishing for. He knows the policy of this government.
The export of water in the massive quantities he is referring to is excluded under the provisions of the free trade agreement. There is nothing wrong with selling bottled water. I hope we sell a lot more of it. There is provision for that as a commodity, but there is certainly no provision for the export of water under the free trade agreement.

Mr. Speaker, the minister has indicated that the government will do something about the bridging requirements for farms for this spring.
In his speech of March 1 and again today, the minister said that those bridging requirements would be tied to enrolment in GRIP and NISA. Is he implying by that statement that farmers who do not sign up in GRIP or NISA cannot expect any help in the bridging period?

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the guidelines that were developed were couched in terms that would hopefully lead to the enrolment of more rather than fewer people in the GRIP and NISA concept.
For the benefit of the hon. member, I will reread the principle to which I think he is referring. One of the criteria is to:
b) build on the objective of the new safety net program and be linked, as far as possible, to participation in the new safety nets;
With respect to delivery, "to the greatest extent possible," programs should be, "delivered through GRIP-NISA delivery systems". That is not only a set of principles which I think we can live with, but the
provinces have endorsed those principles. I am pleased to note that many of the farm organizations which have commented on those principles have also supported them.
It is very difficult when we are trying to develop the basic three lines of defence. The first is the management and operational capabilities of the producer himself, and the responsibility that he or she must take in that regard. Second, the safety net programs which are funded through a sharing arrangement between the federal-provincial and producer communities. The third line of defence effectively kicks in when the first and second do not apply, and when there are unforeseen disasters or problems that are not envisioned or covered by the first two lines of defence. Obviously, if some people believe that the third line of defence is going to be a substitute for the second line of defence, we are going to be back to square one.
I think the hon. member would agree that what we need is a longer term solution to provide the kind of stability and security we need, and hopefully to re-establish the kind of confidence the hon. member and I both want to see in the agriculture community.

I want to explore the same point a little further.
I can see acceptance of the fact that the GRIP and NISA are the first or second line of defence, but the implication in the speech on March 2 was that if a farmer did not have GRIP then he should not expect any help, even if by not taking GRIP he gave up the opportunity for a certain level of support.
However, what we are talking about here is the bridging period. There may not be any payment from GRIP at the end of the year if the prices are high enough, but the bridging period is here and the need is here for that period of time. Any suggestion that if a farmer does not enrol in GRIP he will not get any assistance for the bridging period eliminates all of the voluntary factor in the particular programs, because they are both considered voluntary. They do not become voluntary if we say: "No money for you for last year if you don't enrol in it this year."

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I could pose the question to the hon. member: What would you do next year if we ended
March 18, 1991

up in the same situation, where a person was not enrolled and he again found himself in difficult circumstances, and a good portion of the rest of the producer community became involved in the GRIP and NISA program and found protection? Would the hon. member expect the federal government to come out with another line of defence just to meet the needs of that individual?
That is the balance we have to weigh. We are not attempting compulsion here. What we are trying to do is invite farmers to become part of the solution. We are giving them a mechanism to help themselves. Every time a producer signs up for the program, the federal government is picking up 41-2/3 per cent of the premium and the province is picking up 25 per cent of the premium. The producer is buying 100 cents on the dollar insurance for 33-1/3 cents. It seems to me that it is a pretty good deal.
If we are going to have the kind of stability over the long term, if we are going to have the kinds of management tools that will allow producers to become more self-reliant, that will allow them to make their decisions in advance rather than put their crop in and hope for the best and maybe the federal or provincial government will come to the rescue, it is important to have these kinds of instruments in advance so they can be used as a management tool, as well as the farmer's own expertise and wisdom in terms of the operation of his farm unit.

Mr. Speaker, I want to take this opportunity to say a few words on this resolution.
The resolution asks for immediate action on the part of the government to ensure that funds are in place for planting this year. That is exactly the question I was asking the minister just a few minutes ago in the sense that if this fund is dependent on enrolment, we only have a couple of weeks or a month until the actual seeding begins.
As the minister suggests, if this is to be a tool for survival in farming, then there are a lot of decisions to be made relative to enrolment in the gross revenue fund. If the farmer cannot be sure that he is going to have money to plant this year, there does not seem to be any value in enrolling in GRIP if he is not going to put any seed in the
ground. He is obviously not going to be one of the farmers taking his crop off this year.

Along with other vehicles, such as the Edwards- Beaudoin committee and various provincial task forces, the citizens' forum is trying to do a job to help make Canada work.
Those who seek to destroy the forum and with it the government that established it, without themselves offering constructive, implementable alternatives may in fact be contributing not just to the demise of the citizens' forum but to the demise of Canada.
The future strength and survival of Canada and the quest for unity are legitimate topics for differences of opinion among Canadians. They are not appropriate subjects for partisan politics.
In 1864 a great Liberal leader, George Brown, abandoned partisanship to make Canada work. It is time the opposition in this House did the same.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the tradition of dedicating March as Red Cross month
dates back to 1943. In designating this month, the Red Cross Society in Canada is able to focus its public education campaign to remind people about the very worth-while and necessary work undertaken by the Red Cross, its dependence upon volunteer support and its reliance on the generosity of the public in maintaining services.
Last year alone, an estimated 4 million Canadians benefited from emergency response, health, safety and community programs provided by the Canadian Red Cross. As well, Canadian funds went to relief operations in more than 66 countries including funds to help refugees in the Persian Gulf, and victims of famine in the Horn of Africa.
It should also be noted that the Canadian International Development Agency, through its International Humanitarian Assistance Program, will contribute $1.4 million to the Red Cross for use in Kuwait and Iraq for basic health care needs and water purification equipment.
The Red Cross has as its purpose the alleviation of human suffering. When help is needed in Canada and around the world, the Red Cross responds.
Let us salute the Red Cross, a truly humanitarian international organization.

March 18, 1991

The memo states:
Due to the present Federal Government Budget restraints, we may be forced to operate under present student wage employment programs.
This program is a seasonal rescue program. They work in six separate maritime locations during tourist season.
This program affixes hourly rates of pay to levels of education. For example, a third year community college student in his last year is eligible to only make the equivalent wage scale of a first year university student.
What type of message does this send to the Canadian trades people, the very people who make the country work? A third year community college student warrants only the same wage scale as a first year university student?

Some have said that this government does not care about the civil servants who will have to work in the unemployed centres and look face to face with the unemployed of this nation.

I was witness to that from yesterday's Ottawa Citizen, a quote from "Government Business Opportunities" that the government is putting out a tender for a crowd control system. speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during recent days I met with many farmers in the riding of Macleod. Of course, right now many questions are being asked about the new GRIP program or the Gross Revenue Insurance Plan.
GRIP was designed to protect grain and oilseed producers from shortfalls in revenue, caused by either poor yields or low prices. GRIP is designed to provide protection in an effective, predictable way by basing coverage on individual circumstances.
The program does not mask long-term market trends. Rather, it provides farmers with a buffer against sudden and drastic price changes. It is a welcome long-term response to the needs of farmers. I will continue to work to ensure that this program meets the specific needs of farmers in southwestern Alberta and other parts of Canada.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is a crisis in the agriculture industry today and Canadians do not know about it.
Canadians do not realize that the year 1991 represents a turning point in the Canadian food industry.
The success or failure of this crop year will determine whether or not Canada will have a secure future in agriculture.
Statistics show that there will be a minus 54.5 per cent change in total net farm income in 1991. What industry can sustain such a loss and remain in business?
Yet Canadians demand cheap, environmentally friendly, attractively packaged food on their grocery shelves.
We cannot have it both ways, Mr. Speaker. We cannot have cheap food and profitable farms without assistance from the taxpayer.
We as a nation must realize that unless our farmers survive, we will be dangerously dependent on foreign food supplies. Whether it is the grain industry in the west, the horticulture industry in Ontario, the dairy
March 18, 1991

industry in Quebec, or the potato industry in P.E.I., our food producers have to survive.
Immediate assistance must be made available now if our food industry is to survive into the future.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, multilateral trade negotiations on agriculture will soon resume in Brussels, as part of GATT.
We hope the European Community will want to start serious negotiations on questions affecting agriculture. The Canadian government is convinced, however, that GATT member countries are determined to resolve their differences.
Canadian farmers need improved trade regulations that apply across the board. We must achieve the following objectives: reduce substantially the subsidies that distort world markets; facilitate access to international markets; and verify and reinforce article XI of GATT, in accordance with the proposal made in March by Canadian and Quebec farmers, including minimum levels for access to the Canadian market, in accordance with international obligations.
In concluding, Mr. Speaker, I want to say that we Canadians must defend our position which demands better safeguards for our supply management system. We have made sacrifices, we are disciplined, we have acquired some very valid structures, and we want to keep them.
As far as article XI of GATT is concerned, Canada has so far been able to rally a number of countries to its official position, which is to clarify and strengthen this article.

Mr. Speaker, as another spring approaches, supporters of Canada's only inland sea port at Churchill are again gearing up for a fight to ensure that a fair share of prairie grain is shipped to our overseas customers through this port.
Oral Questions
With the government's dismal lack of financial and moral support and its willingness to encourage rail-line abandonment in the west, it is a wonder how the port has survived. Churchill has tremendous potential as a transportation staging point for shipping goods to Canada's northern communities. Churchill has a role to play in not only maintaining the north, but also in developing it further. Yet last year the government's air terminal was almost forced to close down completely due to neglect, resulting in it being declared a fire hazard.
Many remember the rocket range in Churchill. The National Research Council's site has had a growing interest in the science sector. We have a government report that indicates that with a reasonable marketing strategy, the range could make a profit. But we need a government that is willing to invest in our north.
I call upon the government to start paying attention to what is happening in Canada's north. The community of Churchill is but one example of how hard it is to struggle with resources but without a government with a vision. How many more Churchills are out there in Canada's north?

March 18, 1991

legislation that will provide security, predictability and some stability for the agricultural industry, particularly the grains and oilseeds sector because it is primarily designed around that and that has been the priority of the safety net task force.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
It concerns a colleague of mine and a member of this House, the hon. member for Trinity-Spadina, who went as a member of this House to observe elections in Mexico and has now had his visa cancelled because of the Mexican government's view, probably, that he was
against the free trade agreement and the fraud in that election.
What does the minister intend to do about this incident? Will he tell members of the House whether or not he is prepared to protect the members of this House?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I look forward to hearing from our colleague when he returns.
The hon. member knows that Mexico has a right to revoke visas which it thinks are used for purposes other than the purpose for which they were granted, just as Canada does. When our colleague in the House sought a visa, he did not indicate to Mexican authorities the purpose for which he was planning to make use of that visa. He is still in Mexico. He is there with a tourist visa. He is allowed to stay in the country so long as he respects the term of the visa.
That is the kind of treatment that Canada would apply to people from other countries coming here to whom visas apply. Surely we should not complain if that same kind of treatment is accorded to Canadians who go to countries regarding which visas are required of Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, I regret the embarrassment to the minister, but somebody has misinformed him and should be made aware of the fact that on March 4, this year, the member concerned sent, with a copy to his department, a letter to the Mexican ambassador stating as follows: "I am writing to request a visit to Mexico from March 12th to March 19th as part of a delegation to monitor elections in Morelos State. I will be visiting at the invitation of the PRD."
This is why the Government of Mexico gave him the visa, contrary to what the minister says.
I ask the minister to make a commitment to this House to come back and tell us who misinformed the minister. Second, what will the minister do to protect an MP who said clearly what he intended to go there for in the first place?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will certainly look at that, but let me make a larger point to the House. If it turns out-

speechtext:

If I was misinformed in my answer, I will certainly advise the House of that fact.
There is the other point I want to make. One of the important developments now in the world is that there is an an increasing willingness on the part of countries whose democratic systems Canadians have criticized, to invite election observers in. Canadians are responding formally to that kind of request.
When we have instances where individual members of Parliament go on their own and undertake the kind of activity in which unfortunately two members of this House have been involved in the last week, that can raise serious questions about the effectiveness and the willingness of Canada to take part in what most of us regard as a very welcome new development in countries whose regimes we have criticized being prepared to invite in observers to oversee their electoral processes. The Deputy Prime Minister is well aware that the Canadian parliamentary committee which examined the open skies question unanimously rejected the inclusion of cabotage for American air carriers, namely the ability for American airlines to freely and fully cover the Canadian airspace and in between points.
I ask the Deputy Prime Minister this question. Why did the Minister of Transport last month give a major
Oral Questions
speech in Washington encouraging a new treaty, including full cabotage rights? Will the Deputy Prime Minister now give the government's assurance that the Canadian negotiators will not accept, under any circumstances, the granting of cabotage rights to American air carriers?

Mr. Speaker, my question is again to the Deputy Prime Minister who also was a Minister of Transport at one point. We should not make it any worse.
Given that the option of allowing the giant American carriers to operate freely throughout Canada would mean the death knell for our Canadian industry because we simply cannot compete on an even scale, why will the Deputy Prime Minister not say no to any deal that would include cabotage rights for American carriers? Before going into negotiations, why will he not make cabotage a bottom line for the Canadian interests?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour; Minister of State (Transport)

Cabotage, as my hon. friend should know, is a market entry tool just like seats and gates and he should not get off his rocker until we negotiate the two agreements.

Mr. Speaker, I have another question for the Deputy Prime Minister, the former Minister of Transport. Given that the quality of air service in the regions has deteriorated due to this government's agenda to privatize, and that jet service has been lost in many regional centres, does the Deputy Prime Minister really believe that American carriers will give a hoot about serving Canadians living Dryden,

As the hon. member will be well aware, studies have been done in Canada which indicate no threat to the health of women who use the Meme. We are continuing to follow research that is being done in the United States and to ask for further information about breast implants in Canada.
Should we come into possession of any information suggesting a threat to women's health as a result of breast implants, we would obviously take appropriate action.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is for the same minister.
It seems odd that the U.S. food and drug administration is taking steps to protect women and yet this government is not prepared to do so. The U.S. has already implemented new regulations and the minister responsible for health and welfare has done nothing.
Is the minister more concerned with protecting a U.S. company than he is with protecting Canadian women?

speakeroldname: Hon. Perrin Beatty (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Of course not, Mr. Speaker. The assertions made by the hon. member are simply false.
First of all, what is happening in the United States is they are examining all breast implants, not just the Meme. We will, in turn, be getting that information from the Americans, and looking closely at anything that comes forward. We will also be looking at the decision of the court in New York city as well.
In addition to that, we have taken independent action in Canada to seek information. We will take any action that is necessary to protect the health of Canadian women. That is the commitment we make and it is one that we have kept.
I have also offered to the hon. member and to all other hon. members in the House that if they would like a full briefing on the subject by the scientists in my department, we would be pleased to make arrangements for that.

very recent interval. I think hon. members would want to extend the same courtesy to the hon. minister that have been extended to other members when the matter has been raised.

I recognize that any member of the cabinet can get up and answer a question and that there are ministers designated from time to time to answer questions in the absence of another minister. However, sometimes it makes sense if the person asking the question gets up and says: "In the absence of the Minister of the Environment, I am asking my questions of the minister of energy". There might be a very logical reason for doing that.
I would suggest, Mr. Speaker, as we do quite often, recognizing that we do have rules of the House, that sometimes it makes a lot more sense for common sense to prevail and that in the case quite often when members get up, make reference to the absence of a member or a minister that it really assists the House and certainly assists those people who are watching in the public.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let me first respond to the member for Hamilton West who indicates that he did not state: "In the absence of the Minister of Transport", he may well be right. If I inferred otherwise, I apologize to him.
In terms of his other comments, he made perhaps a very relevant point in commenting that as a relatively new member he is following the examples set. I understand that and it is quite appropriate. I guess my point is that in a variety of ways, through things happening and being duplicated and triplicated and becoming the norm, we have established practices which are being criticized by our own members in terms of the opportunity to ask questions and to respond, and by those who watch in terms of the relevance to the governing of Canada of some of the actions that occur.
In the context of the question raised the other day by the House leader of the Liberal Party as to the question of time, I rose then, and I just repeat today and raised examples today of wherein it may well be appropriate for us to re-examine the definitions of what Question Period is, as stated in Beauchesne, or with those things that are no longer relevant and adopt and enforce those which would be appropriate to what we want to see.
March 18, 1991

Again, the member for Churchill is still here, I would comment with regard to what he suggested, that sometimes it might be appropriate to ask a question "in the absence of", the difficulty is in terms of what it does for the minister who is not there. It says to everybody who is watching: "The minister is not in his seat. He is not in Ottawa." The question, in order to protect the reputation, if you will, to establish that he or she is bona fide involved in government business, presumably invites a session where somebody stands up and says: "While the Minister of the Environment is currently touring the Fraser Valley", and so on and so forth, and to go through that exercise.
My understanding is that is why Beauchesne, and based on previous Speakers' rulings, indicates it is inappropriate to raise the question of the absence of ministers from the House. All I am asking is that until we change that rule, let us enforce, it.

Mr. Speaker, I am somewhat perplexed by the comments of the government House leader today. It has been the practice of this House for some time to put a question in the fashion that he objects to today, to say that in the absence of such and such a minister, I put my question to the Prime Minister or to the Deputy Prime Minister or whatever. I have never heard anyone object to this. Indeed, this formulation is intended to assist cabinet. We know very well that ministers are given the task of responding for other ministers. To me, it has always been the common sense way of drawing attention to the responsibility and getting the attention of perhaps the cabinet minister who had been asked to respond for another.
I really do not know what alternative there would be. I would seek your suggestion, Mr. Speaker, or the advice of the government House leader in this regard. Perhaps one would say my question relates to science and I bring it to the attention of cabinet in the hope that there is someone who is qualified to answer. Maybe he would prefer that.
I think you would agree, Mr. Speaker, that it might be a bit longer and it might take up more time in Question Period to put questions in that fashion.
Point of Order
Again, I really wonder what is behind this. Why did the government House leader raise it in this fashion? Perhaps he has a legitimate point. It seems to me that this kind of matter ought not to be raised without warning on the floor of the House of Commons. These are the kinds of questions where there are other fora for consideration of matters of this nature.
I ask the government House leader perhaps to reconsider his manner of dealing with questions like this.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Perhaps I can be of assistance. When some of us who are in this Chamber first came here, including the government House leader, myself and others who are here-it is getting to be a long time ago-and something happened during Question Period with which another member umbrage, Question Period could be interrupted with a point of order. That was eventually done away with by agreement of all hon. members in order to get on with Question Period.
I am as aware as anybody else in this place that from time to time there are complaints about Question Period, or at least suggestions for its improvement. It comes not only from both sides of the House, but it also comes from the country.
The hon. government House leader has raised a matter and I think the appropriate thing to do is to go back a few days. I certainly appreciate the hon. member for Saint-Henri-Westmount and the very cordial and courteous way in which he has approached this matter. I think it would be helpful if there were some discussions about some of these matters. Certainly I do not think it is appropriate for me today to lay down any dictates. If hon. members want to go back into the past, there were some very clear statements made by past Speakers as to exactly how Question Period should be conducted. Those statements gave a certain degree of constraint on both questions and answers. If the House wishes to come to me and suggest that we make some adjustments to our present practices, as I said the other day, I would certainly be prepared to listen.
I do want to remind hon. members that once upon a time the practice was that if there was a complaint it was taken up in the middle of Question Period. We decided that it ought not to be done at that time. The hon. House leader has raised it subsequent to Question Period, as is the right of all hon. members and he of course has the right to do.

March 18, 1991
Privilege
I would hope that we could have some discussions. I think there is a genuine feeling in the House that Question Period is perhaps a unique institution of our country and a very important one but that we want to make it as effective and as fair as we possibly can. I will look forward to hearing from hon. members in this regard.

speakeroldname: Mr. Vincent Della Noce (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Revenue):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue
subsubtopic: CLARIFICATION OF STATEMENT MADE ON THE JOURNAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today in the House to clarify a statement I made on March 14 on the CBC program The Journal. I apologize for the fact that part of what was broadcast last Thursday may have given a wrong impression of my opinion of native people. I am very sorry if my comments gave the impression that I was referring to native people as a whole. I can assure the House that such was not the case, because what I had in mind was the behaviour of certain warriors during the crisis at Oka last summer, a crisis that left its mark on us all.
I may add that these remarks were made in the context of a conference meeting with a group of social agencies. The meeting was about federalism and Canadian unity. The agencies had an opportunity to talk about the past and about their concerns for the future. It was an open, friendly and public discussion, the kind I regularly have with my constituents and certain business groups.
I want to emphasize that I never expressed any threats of any kind towards any group whatsoever.
And how could I, Mr. Speaker, since these people are important members of my community. Many of them, with whom I have worked for many years, I consider as my friends, because their efforts have helped me to improve the social conditions in my riding.
Mr. Speaker, this array of opinions expressed by 19 groups-not 190, a figure that was referred to out of context in the House and outside the House-may have set the rumour mill going in Ottawa, but we should not judge these opinions out of context. They should be
judged in a context that leaves no room for any misunderstanding.
I only went so far as to mention or point out that curiously, some anti-federal groups have no compunction about cashing cheques from the federal government and wearing a "Participation Quebec" badge. Those are facts, facts that can be checked and were checked.
In concluding, Mr. Speaker, I can give this House the assurance that I am still determined to defend the cause of a united Canada with a strong Quebec, and my efforts will continue, with due respect for all ethnic groups and all persons concerned, and especially for all Quebeckers.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a matter of privilege for which I have given notice.
I would like to quote from Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, Sixth Edition, citation 27, which reads:
A genuine question of privilege is a most serious matter and
should be taken seriously by the Flouse.
I take this matter very seriously. It pertains to the comments just made by the hon. member for Laval-Est, in which I heard no apology to the aboriginal people of Canada.
I would like to quote from the transcript of the comments of the hon. member, which reads:
It's like the Indians. They don't like our laws, they don't respect
this, they don't respect the Constitution, but they want to have the
money.
This matter deals with remarks about aboriginal people made by the hon. member last Thursday, March 14, on CBC's The Journal. I respectfully submit that my privilege as a member of Parliament has been breached and that a contempt of Parliament has thus occurred. The hon. member's statements reflect on the House as a whole and reflect on individual members thereof, namely the aboriginal members of this House.
According to Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, Sixth Edition, at page 11, parliamentary privilege is enjoyed by individual members and by each House for the protection of its members and the vindication of its own authority and dignity.
March 18, 1991

I submit that the hon. member's statements impinge on my ability and that of the other aboriginal MPs in this House to do their jobs properly. We have been misrepresented, and these remarks are derogatory not only to us but to the dignity of the entire House of Commons.
Mr. Joseph Maingot, in Parliamentary Privilege in Canada, stated at page 213:
There are actions which, while not directly in a physical way
obstructing the House of Commons or the member, nevertheless
obstruct the House in the performance of its functions by diminishing
the respect due it.
I respectfully submit that respect for this House has been diminished in two ways by the comments of the hon. member for Laval-Est. Again I refer to the transcripts of The Journal, and I would like to table this with the Clerk.
First, the member's comments were racially based and discriminatory against aboriginal people in Canada. The elimination of racism and prejudice-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Not to take anything away from the issue, whatever the member's complaint is, an hon. member has got up and said that under no circumstances did he mean it to be a slight against any of the people of Canada.
Second, I have to apply the rules in this as I would have to apply them in any other case. It is very difficult for me, despite the complaint the hon. member may have, to see how this in any way impinges upon his ability to do his duty as a member of Parliament in this House or anybody else's ability to do their duty.
What we have here clearly is a remark. The hon. member has stood in his place and we have to accept in this place the hon. member's word that he was not referring to all of the aboriginal peoples of our country. He was referring to a specific thing and he has made it very clear. I certainly have accepted what he said as making it very clear that he is not insulting nor is he casting aspersions on any group of Canadians, and certainly not aboriginal Canadians.
I have to say to the hon. member that the complaint is made. I see the hon. member for Shefford wants to rise on this matter. It will have to be a very pertinent statement indeed because I am in the midst of saying that there may be a complaint here. If there was, it has
Privilege
been met by an hon. member on the other side and it is not a question of privilege.
The hon. member for Shefford, very briefly. I am bowing of course to the fact that he is a senior member here.

speakerposition: Bloc Québécois House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think that if you look at the comments made by the hon. member for Laval-Est, you will realize that he withdrew his insulting remarks about certain native people but did not withdraw all comments that were specifically directed to sovereigntists, a group to which I belong. In his comments, he said they did not respect the Constitution-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons

He may or he may not have. This place is an adversary forum and we all know that. There are going to be lots of things said that are political. The hon. member has certainly got up and, to my satisfaction, has said that he did not mean an insult and if that is the way it appeared he clearly did not want it to be so.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons

Just a moment. What exactly were the remarks and in what way is it a question of privilege?
There is a big difference between complaining about something and having a question of privilege. The essence of privilege which goes back hundreds of years is: Has somebody done something that makes it impossible or makes it less likely or less able for an individual member to carry on his or her duties as a member of Parliament to speak freely? That is what privilege is.
Hon. members may complain about all kinds of things that we say about each other in this place. It is not necessarily privilege. I would ask the hon. member to tell me just exactly what was said and why it is a question of privilege.
