speechtext: At the suspension of the debate at 2 p.m. the hon. member for Saskatoon- Humboldt had the floor. He has 18 minutes left.

Mr. Speaker, the motion before us is one calling on the government to take action regarding the lack of income for this particular year. It puts before this House the problem of funding for the seeding of the crop in this particular year.
It is a laudable motion, something that we would support. However, if one looks at the record of the government, one also has to think that maybe it is a motion that is a little bit futile. Last year when this government promised that we would have a certain amount of assistance by spring work, many of us were still waiting for it when we harvested the crop that it was supposed to help seed.
The minister, in answering a question just before Question Period, when he made his presentation to this House, also indicated that there was likely to be a considerable hold-up, because he attached all of the bridging funding to the GRIP and NISA programs. Therefore, it is a little difficult to believe that this government is going to do anything for the farmers in time for them to be able to use the assistance for the planting of crops this year.
This government has made it clear that what it intends to do as far as agriculture is concerned is to commit the industry to a market system, a trading system, and a financial system which makes it unlikely the first two of these three systems will allow the farmers enough income so that they can make a living comparable to most other parts of the economy.
The Minister of Agriculture and the government generally make a great song and dance about the fact that we must be competitive, we must fit ourselves into the market system. They make a great song and dance about getting away from direct support to the farmer. Their theme has been to put in place a safety net which
March 18, 1991

would guarantee the farmers enough return for them to survive in farming.
Mr. Speaker, it all sounds very good, and it may even help somebody. But the government, for all its great propaganda about how it has always come to the aid of the farmer and how it will do so in the future-and we heard that again during Question Period today-it has not improved the position of the farmer relative to income in the last six years.
If you were to look at the structure of the income of farmers in today's dollars, you would find that it has gone down considerably-the income has gone down considerably-even with the increase in aid that the government has given them. I am sure you would find it very difficult to find a farmer who would say they are better off today than they were six years ago. I am sure if you went out and asked, that you would have no one volunteer that they are in a better position now than they were six years ago. Certainly, there is no one in the industry who would indicate that is the position they would take.
During the last six years, this government has dispersed among farmers a considerable amount of help in the form of debt review boards, has written off the deficit for the Western Grain Stabilization, and has also expended the amount of money it has given in direct assistance.
But, after all that, we find an industry that is much worse off than it was six years ago.
So, Mr. Speaker, we come to the position that we find ourselves in today. We look at last year's income and we find that it was considerably less than the cost of production. In other words, a large portion of the farmers who were in the industry last year did not make as much as they spent. Even after the government assistance was in place, they did not make as much as they spent. It is predicted that the 1991-1992 crop year will also produce less income than it did last year. The GRIP and NISA plans are supposed to take that up, but the GRIP and NISA plans do not come into effect until the end of this year.
Most industries, if they had that kind of return for several years for their efforts would have curled up and quit. The farmers are a different breed. They go on
Supply
producing. They hope that society recognizes they are contributing something of considerable value and will, therefore, make sure that they can survive.
I suppose, to a certain extent, we have done this. However, there are far fewer farmers now than there were a few years ago. The quality of life in the farm communities is lowering considerably each year.
As I said, society should recognize that farmers contribute considerably to the community. They produce much of the food we eat. There is good reason to believe society would do this. Besides the fact they are producing a considerable amount of the food eaten in Canada, the agricultural industry contributes what we call-I cannot quite come up with the word-but for every dollar paid to the farmer, there is about $7 generated within the general economy. Multiplier is the word I was looking for. This multiplier factor should be recognized by society as a good reason to keep the farmers on the land producing food.
Every farm job kept in place produces quite a large number of other jobs. I can give some examples. These are not direct multipliers, but they give some indication of the effect the farm community has on industry in Canada.
For instance, bread is usually the main product we think of from the farm community. A grain producer gets about 4 cents for the wheat used in a loaf of bread that costs anywhere from $1 to $1.50. That gives a multiplier of something around 33.
A farmer gets 1 cent for the barley used to make a $2 bottle of beer.
Cooking oil, from canola-which is one of the healthiest cooking oils on the market-the farmer gets 60 cents for the canola used in a litre of canola oil which will sell at something over $2.
Even something as simple as sugar cookies, the farmer gets 2 cents for the wheat used in cookies and those cookies are usually worth about $3.
Rye whisky produces a considerable amount of income for the government; it is more often called Canadian whisky in this part of the country. The farmers get 1 cent for the rye that is used in a 40 ounce bottle of whiskey. Most of that multiplier, if you wish, is paid as taxation to the government.

March 18, 1991
Supply
I grant that these multipliers I have mentioned here are not direct, because other products are used in the making of making of the products sold. Consequently, there is not a direct relationship.
It gives us an indication of the impact agriculture has on other industries. For instance, the oats that are used in a $4.88 package of oat bran flakes will only bring the farmer about a cent and a half. Society should recognize that we owe a lot to the farmer in other jobs and in other activity in the community.
To a great extent, the point that is being made here by most of us who are part of the agricultural industry is that agricultural production is important. If we do not pay enough for the product for the farmer to survive, it means that we are reducing the effectiveness of the economy to some extent.
As long as the farmer keeps producing, the rest of the industry can survive. We cannot expect farmers to go on indefinitely producing at a loss. Consequently, eventually we will be looking to other countries for the products that we now buy at home.
If we think of a multiplier factor of seven times for every dollar paid to a farmer, we recognize that agriculture has a major impact upon the economy of the country. Also, it is one of the major suppliers of foreign currency to our government.
The government tells us that it has been helping the farmers with special programs and in other ways for many years. We will grant that it has, but its plan was not to help the industry. It has not helped the industry, because the industry is still going downhill.
For example, during 1989-90, even with government help, the farmers did not recover all of their costs. In 1990-91, unless the government gives them some direct help, the amount of income will be less than it was last year. What they need now are contributions directly, which will give them enough cash so that they can plant their crops this spring.
When the Minister of Agriculture spoke a little while ago in answer to a question we put to him, he said that the government will do something when it is able to do so and when it has enough involvement in the GRIP and NISA plan.
On several occasions over the last year, farm organizations had pressed the Minister of Agriculture to make a
statement on whether or not he was going to assist the farmers in bridging the gap between last year's shortfall in income and the establishment of the GRIP and NISA programs. It was well known for some time that that gap in income was going to be there. The farmers have been asking the minister and the Government of Canada what they intended to do about this gap. Again, that is what is being asked today in this motion.
The minister stated: "Leave it until after we have solved the safety net problem." That might have been some relief to somebody, but it did not assure anybody that they were going to get any funds.
The minister also stated: "We have always helped the farmers when they needed it. We will do so in the future." He made that statement again today, and again there was no commitment to funds for the bridging process.
Later on he said that any answer to this question would be correlated with the GRIP or the NISA program. In the process of making that statement, he indicated to us that he was making it dependent upon the GRIP or the NISA program. In fact he almost threatened-and he did not renege from that position when I asked him the question today-that if people do not join GRIP, they cannot expect to have any assistance. The assistance required is for this year. GRIP is going to pay for next year. It is very unusual or very disturbing to find the government saying that if you do not sign up for GRIP and NISA, which will do you for next year, it will not pay you anything this year.
The first ministers have announced that the GRIP and NISA papers will be complete for the spring work. They also said that if the farmer needs help, the government will pay it. I am sure that John Wise, who promised these GRIP and NISA programs back in 1985-not in those particular words-must be breathing a little easier, because after all this time we have them in place. However, there is nothing in the programs that deals with the basic fact that money will be there when they need it this spring.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with interest to my colleague's speech on the motion today. I could not help but reflect that over the years that I have had the privilege of sitting in this House, we have

March 18, 1991

experienced and participated in many debates with respect to problems within the Canadian farming community. Almost all of these problems revolve around scarcity of money, lack of funds, lack of income, or incomes that are falling and have been falling over a period of many years.
Today a way of life that at one time, and indeed historically in our country, had a great deal of built-in security based almost entirely on one's ability to work or determination to work has changed to a way of life that is pretty much on the fringe, materially speaking. Farming today is almost a way of life to be avoided. It is very sad and tragic that one of the great pillars of Canadian society, the rural way of life, and farmers in general, is in such an unstable situation and that young people, by and large, bom on farms today do not want to continue farming. I should not say they do not want to continue farming; they fear going into farming because of this lack of security and this inability to live a reasonably secure life based on one's determination and ability to work.
In what way or ways would a New Democratic Party government in Ottawa be different in its approach to assisting farmers, both individually and through their organizations, in respect of these various funding programs that we have debated from time to time in this Chamber? We have seen both Liberal programs and Conservative programs and though they have had the immediate stop-gap effect of preventing ultimate disaster on the farm front, they have not in terms of long-term solutions amounted to very much.
In what way or ways would our party's farm policy differ basically from that of the Liberals and the Conservatives?

Mr. Speaker, I agree that there has been a lack of long-term programming. I give credit to this government for suggesting the GRIP, a program which suggests that there may be long-term assistance in place.
The shortcoming of the GRIP program which is placed before this Elouse is that there is not written into it any cost of production. It will only supply the needs of the farmer as long as the moving average of 15 years is higher than the cost of production. There is no guarantee that is going to happen; in fact, it looks as if within
Supply
two or three years that moving average will be lower than that.
We have a program that we have had as a policy for a good number of years very similar to this, except that the basis of it is the cost of production. For a minimum amount produced by each farmer, a certain portion of his crop, he would be assured the cost of production. Beyond that he would have to depend on the market. Only his insurance would allow him to survive, or to be sure he was going to get some return beyond that, if there was a drought or a bad year.
I suppose one could say that the program we would put in place is not that much different than the GRIP, except that it would have built into it a cost of production, and would have a cap which would not allow a situation as they have in the United States where 85 per cent of the funding from these kinds of programs goes to approximately 10 per cent of the farmers. That kind of a program has a tendency to eliminate more farmers than the number it assists.
The approach that we have been suggesting for many years, and which we hoped John Wise would suggest back in 1985-because we had talked it over with him on many occasions-would establish a program that would allow a return to the farmer at a cost of production level for a certain portion of his crop. He would always be sure that he was going to get some return.
This program does not do that. GRIP does not do that.
NISA under the government is really only a glorified savings plan, and again is only there for the farmers who have extra money. It is so glorified, in fact, that I have had farmers come to me and say: "You know, I think I am going to borrow some money and put it into this NISA plan, because the return on it is better than what it would cost me to borrow the money". That in itself is a discredit to the reason for the plan being put in place.
Basically our plan would not be too much different. But it would assure a return to the farmer based on his cost of production and would assure that some farmers were not able to take advantage of it more than others.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a comment to my hon. friend from Saskatoon-Humboldt and perhaps pose a question.

March 18, 1991
Supply
Let me say first that I appreciate his recognition of the fact that there has been some considerable magnitude in the dimension of support to Canadian agriculture by this government, and that he does see elements of merit in the long-term safety net programs which are presently in front of the agriculture committee even as we speak, and soon hopefully back in front of this House.
I want to ask the hon. member a couple of questions relating to the idea of a cost of production formula, and also the idea of some form of support being based on, I gather, the first x number of bushels of production.
In the latter case, I am wondering how he would ensure that there would not be such a proliferation of permit books that in fact all of the production would be qualifying for the additional support that he envisions. I am also wondering how he could apply a cost of production formula into an area like the production of wheat where we are dependent on export for probably 82 per cent or 83 per cent of all of the production in Canada. How is it possible to apply a cost of production and recover that from an international market where, because of factors that lie beyond our borders, there simply is not the return at the present time?

Mr. Speaker, the proliferation of permit books or quota books is a concern that this government is having right now and will have with the program it has put before us.
I would first point to the U.S. programs of conservation where they have managed, very successfully, to control the number of acres. Now they have not managed to control the production particularly well but they have managed to control the number of acres that a particular farm seeds and puts on the market.
We have discussed the questions that he talks about on many occasions. We have felt that it was a minor concern, but the situation where one unit produces or farms 100,000 acres and gets the cost of production for all of that would not happen. That is the main concern for what may happen under the GRIP program.
The second question that he asks is the extent to which the program can be dependent upon. We feel that its greatest weakness is the fact that it is bound to go below
the cost of production within two years unless the price of grain goes up. What you do by putting in place a market controlled level is guarantee that within a certain number of years the price that the farmer gets for his grain will be lower than the cost of production. It will not make any difference how well you farm or how good you are at it. You will still lose money.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Before resuming debate, it is my duty, pursuant to Standing Order 38, to inform the House that the questions to be raised tonight at the time of adjournment are as follows: the hon. member for Lambton-Middlesex-Agriculture; the hon. member for Prince George-Bulkley Valley-Softwood Lumber; the hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond-Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.
Resuming debate.

Mr. Speaker, it is my pleasure to continue the debate this afternoon on the Liberal opposition day resolution. To refresh the memories of those here, it reads as follows:
That this House call upon the Government to take immediate action to deal with drastically reduced farm incomes resulting from the 1990-91 crop year and to make required assistance available in time for spring planting to ensure viable returns for grains, oilseeds and horticultural producers.
It is my pleasure, as I said, to speak to this issue, an agricultural emergency that exists in our country at this time. As others have said, although we have dealt in this House many times over the years with issues of agriculture, we always seem to have an agricultural industry that is in a state of emergency. The state of emergency derives, I believe, from many factors, but one of the major factors for the emergency that exists today is the lack of understanding on the part of the Canadian public in general to the importance of agriculture as a part of our Canadian economy.
Agriculture in Canada today is a $43 billion industry. Since 1988, it has declined from about a $50 billion industry. At the base of that $43 billion industry today, the basic pillar is comprised of our farmers across this country. It is my regret and the regret of many of us who are concerned about agriculture in this country that the number of farmers is declining rapidly and drastically. Western farmers across our prairies had not too bad a
March 18, 1991

year last year only because of good growing conditions and a good crop yield as a result of that.
As we know, before last year they suffered very severely from drought. It is not to say that this past year, for being a better year, has brought them out of the serious financial crisis that they experienced the previous years. They are still suffering from that and they still need considerable assistance in order to survive. The fact is that many have gone bankrupt and many are on the verge of bankruptcy.
I have heard from colleagues in my own caucus, colleagues who represent the ridings of Essex-Kent and Haldimand-Norfolk, as well as ridings in southwestern Ontario who are experiencing severe agricultural problems at this time. Farmers are giving up because they have lost crops and the prices for their commodities have dropped considerably. They do not have the funds to produce crops this year; vegetable growers to get seed into the ground and fruit producers to get the spray on their fruit and other crops that they might have.
We are in serious trouble across this country. We have heard of the potato farmers in Prince Edward Island as well as other horticultural producers in the east part of our country. They all are crying and begging for assistance.
This government has tried in different ways to address the needs of farmers across this country. At the present time, with spring planting coming on, particularly for horticultural producers, there is a gap. There is an emergency need, a crisis at this time, for our government to address this issue and to allow our horticultural producers to get on stream to get their crops yielding for this current year.
Within the last couple of weeks we started a debate on Bill 098, the Farm Income Protection Act, a comprehensive act which includes insurance programs, income security programs like GRIP and NISA. I think, as I sit here as a non-agricultural expert, one of the reasons perhaps that the Canadian public does not seem to understand and stand behind agricultural producers, our fanners in this country, is that we use terminology which is really unknown to most Canadians.
Supply
As I speak today, I will try to avoid using terms like GRIP and NISA, but simply to explain that, as I said before, these are income security programs, insurance programs meant to help and assist with income security for farmers across this country. Those programs are very important.
I stood here last week and applauded the minister for the method that he used in bringing the bill forward in the House. He combined farmers and provincial and federal government officials in the discussions out of which came the proposed Farm Income Protection Act, that we will presumably be voting upon within the next week or so.
The Farm Income Protection Act, although it might have many points of great merit within it, does not provide the type of assistance which horticultural producers in this country require at this time. There are 20,000 horticultural producers, producers of vegetables and fruit, in this country. Half of those producers, 10,000 of them, reside in Ontario.
Last week, as has been mentioned here in the House before, the Ontario Fruit and Vegetable Growers' Association appeared before the Standing Committee on Agriculture and outlined the problems that their industry is facing at this time. They indicated that the Ontario producers alone require $700 million this year in order to produce their crops for this year.
They do not see how they can be assisted at this time by the Farm Income Protection Act that is before the House right now. It is an act which provides for insurance and income security programs for the year 1991-1992. They want to be assured, as well as the grains and oilseeds producers who will benefit from that program, that if they receive any income support this year or insurance coverage this year it will not be seen as a prepayment for the 1991-1992 crop year, because we are talking about the needs of the previous year and we cannot be continually playing catch-up.
On the other hand, producers do not like the ad hoc programs that are constantly being put in place and have had to be put in place to help them. At this point there seems to be no other possible, but yet there is one more ad hoc program for this year, particularly for horticultural producers who have such great need.
From what I can understand, one of the problems with the producers is that under one section of the Agriculture Income Protection Act the GRIP is fairly easily

March 18, 1991
Supply
defined for grains and oilseed producers, but it is much more difficult to define for our horticultural industry. Our fruit and vegetables growers produce over 100 different crops and each crop has different parameters. They must work out a separate type of program of insurance and income security. They have not even yet determined what the premiums would be for the various crops that might be covered under that program.
We heard from the minister today-and it would be of concern to the horticultural producers-that they may receive nothing this year in emergency assistance unless they become part of the GRIP program now for 1991-1992. Even if horticultural producers have the funding in hand to pay a premium, they do not know how that program will benefit them and the crops they produce. There are definitely problems and deficits in the legislation as it stands at this time, particularly for horticultural producers.
On the weekend I was reading the newspaper put out by the Ontario fruit and vegetable producers called The Grower. It had an article which referred to our agriculture minister's video speech to the B.C. Fruit Growers Association last month via satellite. We heard different members talk in the House today about a third line of defence committee, but for the average Canadian citizen I am afraid again that this would just be so much Greek and they would not really understand what that was referring to. I did not understand completely what it was referring to until I read this veiy good article in this agricultural newspaper.
It mentioned the first line of defence, which our minister referred to today, the second line of defence and the third line of defence. Our horticultural producers are saying that they need assistance from the third line of defence committee immediately in order that they can work this spring.
Just to explain to the Canadian public who may be tuned in to the House of Commons today, the first line of defence refers specifically to what is possible for producers themselves to do for themselves to promote their own self-sufficiency, and programs the Canadian and provincial governments can become involved in as well to help support our farmers across this country to become more self-sufficient. It looks toward farmers being as efficient as they possibly can be in production.
Certainly it has been seen in past years that farmers have indeed become much more efficient in their production methods than was perhaps previously the case.
However, in line with the first line of defence there are responsibilities the government must take as well. One of the most important ones in this era of free trade with the United States is for our government to help our Canadian farmers to be able to compete in the international markets on a level playing field.
Last week, when horticultural producers came before the Standing Committee on Agriculture, they outlined some of the problems they experience that cause them not to be able to compete fairly with American farmers. For example, we cannot get registered in Canada certain chemicals used on fruit to help the preservation and quality of crops that are grown in United States but are imported into this country.
In the United States they have a spray that deals with a disease called the pear psylla. This spray has not been registered here and cannot be used by Canadian pear producers. We are in serious condition of losing pear production in this country because this fact alone is causing our pear farmers not to be able to compete.
I come from a region that is famous for its apple production. I invite members and the Canadian public to come to the great riding of Northumberland to experience our delicious apples in the fall. Apple producers in Northumberland have come to me and have spoken of their problem of not being able to acquire in Canada registered chemicals that are available in the United States. This therefore lowers the quality, the saleability and the pricing. It is a detriment to them when it comes to selling their product in Canada, to say nothing of trying to export and sell their product abroad. It must be remembered that although we have a $43 billion agrifood industry in Canada, we export about 25 per cent of that agrifood production. That in itself accounts for about one-third of Canada's trade balance.
We are not talking about a minor economic sector in our economy. In fact the food industry from farm to supermarket is one of Canada's largest economic sectors. The sector, the bottom tier of which is our farming community, includes many other workers in the agrifood industry as has been mentioned before. It would include our transportation of food sector, the producer sector,
March 18, 1991

the marketing sector, the advertising sector, and the sales and supermarkets of which we are all aware.
For $1 of produce at the farm gate there is an additional $7 brought into the Canadian economy as a result of that $1 of farm production in this country. The importance of farmers to the economy of this country simply cannot be underestimated.
Many Canadians do not really understand the importance of agriculture in this country and the fact that there are so many farmers who are going out of business and experiencing bankruptcy in these days. Statistics were referred to earlier here today, that Agriculture Canada predicts the total net farm income in Canada will drop by 54.5 per cent this year as compared with last year, and that only three provinces in this country will have a positive net farm income in 1991. Saskatchewan and Manitoba will have the most difficult time. well. Ontario and Quebec will also have very difficult times.
From my point of view it is very difficult to start comparing sectors in the farming economies that are experiencing rougher or tougher times than another. If a farmer cannot make it, the situation is critical. It is of great concern to me that in my own riding of Northumberland I have seen several farmers in the last few years go out of business. These are farmers who have good university education. Some of them are fortunate enough to have come home from university to land that was held by their family for generations. With good equipment, with all of these resources in hand -and I know these people to be excellent business people-they are unable to make their farms economically viable and have had to leave their farms.
Much earlier in my life I came from the Burlington region. I watched that region of our country get gobbled up as farm land was sold by farmers who found it more economically feasible to sell their land to developers. I personally never want to see that happen to other areas of our country, but unfortunately I do continue to see it happen. It is something that we must stop as quickly as possible.
The agricultural industry in Canada faces many challenges, not least of which is the challenge of international trade. Canada does subsidize its food industry, but it is
Supply
not recognized by the Canadian public that in fact we pay very little for our food in comparison to its actual costs. But as we subsidize our industry we are competing with the U.S. and European countries that subsidize even more heavily. It is very hard for Canadian farmers to receive less; it is impossible for Canadian farmers to receive less for their production than they do nowadays.
I know this government is aware of the difficulties and is trying to deal with international trade issues, but we cannot stop. We must continue to do everything possible to try to support and help our agricultural food industry.
We laugh when we hear children being told or coming forward with the understanding that the stork brings babies. I very much get the impression that many citizens in Canada do not think beyond the supermarket when it comes to thinking of where food comes from, what the source of their food is.
Canadians must regard the crisis we have in the agricultural industry in our country at this time as their crisis and something that we all together must understand and try to do something about.
I have had the good fortune of browsing through a book called Farming the System by Mr. Barry K. Wilson, which gives a very good review of how politicians and producers shape Canadian agricultural policy. It is something I would recommend to all Canadian citizens to read in order to understand more about the agricultural industry in this country and what we can all do to help to improve the policies that we have in support of our farmers. They need our help. They need our understanding.
Politicians are going to be able to respond in a better way if all Canadian citizens become better informed and let politicians, decision makers, legislation makers, know that they understand the needs of the agricultural industry in this country and the enormous importance of agriculture to the economy and security of this country.

Mr. Speaker, I wanted to pick up on a comment that the hon. member for Northumberland just made. I think she quite properly raised the matter that there is a lack of understanding or a gulf between urban dwellers and farm people or producers today.

March 18, 1991
Supply
She used the analogy of the stork bringing babies. Indeed I think when a lot of people go to the supermarket they do not realize that the food and the produce on the shelves come in fact from real live people, most of them Canadian.
If anything, there is a widening of this gulf, a heightened lack of understanding on the part of many Canadians as to exactly where their food does come from. In fact we in Canada enjoy the second lowest cost of food in the world. It is clear that some of the reason for that is the return that Canadian producers receive.
It has always troubled me that every program which the government announces on behalf of agriculture, whether it is crop insurance payments or WGSA payments or even the Canadian Wheat Board final payment, which in fact is entirely the producer's own money, is given a great headline in the media with a suggestion that it is another handout to the farm community. That in turn is seen by urban residents in a negative way.
That is why I rather like the concept of moving to these long-term safety net programs, GRIP and NISA, which are in fact in front of the House now and are moving forward. I wonder if the hon. member for Northumberland would agree with me that those programs will be a step in the right direction not only for their content, but also by lessening the dependence that we have had on ad hoc programs and all of the negative publicity that seems to come with each one. I wonder if the hon. member would agree that to the extent these programs will replace ad hockery and to the extent that they are permanently in place they will reduce the need for ad hoc programs and thereby reduce the kind of publicity which seems to widen the understanding between rural and urban areas.

Mr. Speaker, yes, I would agree. Earlier I was talking about the different lines of defence, the jargon used currently around the House. I talked about the first line of defence and the second line of defence being the Farm Income Protection Act, that type of long-term program which I do think is important. I think we have to keep reviewing that type of program, which I understand the minister is prepared to do to make sure that it really does address the changing and emerging needs of the farming community.
What I did not mention was the third line of defence, which is also part of the total farm strategy. The quotes from this paper are saying: "Where the first and second lines of defence do not fully deal with an income problem, the third line of defence would then come into play, the minister explained. This would involve emergency assistance or transitional assistance and it may include input cost". This is the type of program that the horticultural producers in this country today are asking for and are very concerned about.
Although we need solid, long-term programs of assistance, I think that we always are going to require this third line of defence. When the minister meets with the third line of defence committee in the coming couple of weeks, I hope that he will address this urgent need particularly of horticultural producers at this time and understand their needs. They cannot at this time become enrolled in GRIP because of the uncertainty of what that means to the horticultural producers, but in order for them to be able to enrol eventually in that program they need emergency assistance today, which is the third line of defence.

Mr. Speaker, my colleague, the hon. member for Northumberland, spoke about sprays and chemicals that are used on produce to make it last longer while it is being shipped into Canada. Of course, these usually hit our markets at a time when a lot of our own fresh produce is coming on the market or even during the winter months when some of our greenhouse crops are being harvested.
I am very concerned about this same issue because even though some of these chemicals may be banned in Canada, they are used in other countries. Therefore, we do not allow any tolerance for these chemicals on our domestically produced food, but there is a tolerance allowed on imported food, which naturally gives them a competitive advantage coming on to our markets.
I am just wondering if my colleague would like to comment on this and if she thinks the use of these chemicals should be banned. Should we bring in regulations where all foods, both domestic and imported, should have the chemical content, pesticide, herbicide and so on, listed when they are put on sale in the supermarkets so that the Canadian consumer knows exactly what she is buying?
March 18, 1991

Mr. Speaker, I believe that my colleague brings up a very good point. When I was speaking to that particular issue and the role of government, I was talking again about the first line of defence and the need for our producers to have a level playing field. At the same time as we want to have a level playing field, we have Canadian standards of health and acceptability with regard to chemicals.
Some chemicals that may be acceptable by American standards are not necessarily acceptable by Canadian standards. There is an urgent need for the government to act quickly to determine which of the chemicals are used on products in the United States that are imported into Canada are acceptable for consumption in Canada and which ones are not. If chemicals used on products imported into this country from the United States are acceptable, then they must be immediately registered in Canada so that Canadian farmers have equal access and equal opportunity to use them.
I have had complaints, as well, from organic farmers who try not to use chemicals. They use more natural substances. Who knows, maybe they are as toxic as regular chemicals. I cannot be the judge of that. But many people have spoken to me about this serious problem. So it is to have a level playing field, but a level playing field based upon Canadian standards of health and well being.
I also think it is important for all of our food products, whether they are imported or not, whether they are sprayed natural products or processed products, should be well marked in stores what chemicals are used so that consumers know what they are ingesting.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in this debate, actually against the motion put by the opposition and, of course, in support of the government's agricultural record. I will try to do so from the perspective of a member who represents an area of some 25,000 square miles in southwestern and south central Saskatchewan, which is very dependent upon agriculture, especially, the grains sector and particularly the production and export of wheat.
There is no question that Canadian farmers and, especially at this time, the grains and oilseed producers
Supply
are faced with unprecedented circumstances. There has been enormous pressure to change and to adapt and that, in fact, is happening. We continue to support the farm community as we have always done, to help them meet their challenges at home and in the international marketplace.
There are three particular ways in which the government can assist the grains and oilseeds sector. The first is on the international level, where through the negotiations in GATT and with the Cairns group and with other nations, we tiy to bring about, if not an end, at least a lessening of the harmful subsidies which have so drastically affected the international price which our producers depend upon.
The second area is in regard to domestic agriculture. We must try to retain those things that were good out of the old agricultural programs and try to repair those deficiencies through innovations such as the GRIP and NISA programs which have developed a new generation of green sector safety nets, developed by the grain safety net committee.
The third area we should be addressing is that of diversification. When I say diversification, I mean within agriculture and, indeed, outside. Agricultural diversification is good, but it is obviously not possible to shift some 600 miles of prairie for which the highest and best use appears to be wheat production, into something else. It is just not feasible and not practical.
Progress is being made through Western Economic Diversification to diversify in a non-agricultural sense. We are trying to support and enable enterprises that have new products, new ideas, new technology, new markets, a possibility of import replacement to flourish on the prairies so that it will be possible to have plants, factories and initiatives which will employ prairie people in areas and occupations and walks of life that are not so dependent upon agriculture, as is the case at the present time.
Since the mid-1980s the federal government has provided an unprecedented level of income support to the grain and oilseeds sector, about $12 billion in direct assistance. This support has been delivered through record high pay-outs under existing programs such as the WGSA, that is the western grain stabilization program and through special programs that responded to unexpected emergencies.

March 18, 1991
Supply
Long-term programs like western grain stabilization were put in place to provide stability to producers and it has served that purpose well. However, it was never intended to deal with the kind of emergencies the industry faced during the late eighties and today. One obvious flaw was that the triggering mechanism was for the entire Canadian Wheat Board area rather than for specific areas. Another flaw was the five-year rolling average of income, which is fine when there is a quantum shift from one year to the next, but is not much good when the prices drop consistently and over a five-year period show very little change.
The problem is that farmers could no longer rely on these programs for predictable support. They indicated they needed a more effective and predictable safety net program, and that is why the legislation enabling GRIP and NISA, the Farm Income Protection Act, is now before this House. It is hoped that these programs, which were recommended to the government by the Grain Safety Net Committee composed in the majority of producers, will answer some of the problems.
The difficulty we find ourselves in, all Canadians and the grain producers in particular, is the trade subsidy war, the grain export subsidy war which has developed through the mid-eighties and late eighties between the European Economic Community and the United States. The Europeans, since the sixties, have been heavily subsidizing the production and eventually the over-production of product, including grain. They have embarked upon programs to subsidize the further export of their excess production.
The United States suffered a diminution of its share of the market for a number of years as a result of the European activities and eventually the Americans took the gloves off and got into the subsidy battle as well. Unfortunately, Canadian producers have been caught in the cross-fire. It has been particularly difficult because, as we all know, the European Economic Community has some 330 million people, the United States some 250 million people. We in Canada have 27 million people.
On the other side of the coin, the Europeans are able, because of that population, to consume by far the greater part of their production, so they are exporting-or perhaps I should say dumping on the world market-perhaps 15 per cent of their production.
The United States is in a somewhat similar position, and I am guessing at this point because I have forgotten the numbers, but I suspect that they export well under one-half of their production.
Canadians remain exposed to the tune of about 83 per cent, to export. We consume, as humans, about 7 per cent of our wheat production. Livestock take up perhaps another 9 per cent or 10 per cent. The remainder has to be exported, and that is where our producers are very much at risk.
This subsidy war is being very much fought with a double-edged sword. The big powers, the Europeans and the Americans, have the population to be able to chew up a lot of their production and at the same time they have the population base and the tax base to be able to afford the kind of massive export subsidies that they are affording their producers. So it is a very difficult situation. As a result, international grain prices have dropped dramatically through the eighties to the point now where, as we speak, as a result of some recent sales, it appears that the international price-if one can call it that-is in the area of $1.50 to $1.75 per bushel of wheat. Clearly, Canadian producers face a major problem. This is something that has been building for some time.
This has not gone unanswered. We, of course, recall the Canadian Special Grains Program in 1986, under which $1 billion was paid out to Canadian producers in addition to the regular government programs. The following year another $1.1 billion was paid out through that program.
Prices did recover somewhat in 1988 so that there was no need to extend the Special Grains Program, but just when we thought we could see some light at the end of the tunnel another crisis arose. In 1988 we had a drought which caused difficulty and suffering to many parts of Canada. The prairies, parts of southern Ontario and Quebec suffered the most severe drought since the 1930s. Crop losses were significant in many areas. Again this government responded with the Canadian Crop Drought Assistance Program which injected some $850 million into the farm economy. In addition, there was a Livestock Drought Assistance Program and a Green Feed Program in western Canada which put out another almost $150 million.
|

March 18, 1991

As I indicated earlier, Canada cannot hope to match the treasuries of the United States and Europe but, at the same time, we cannot allow farmers to fend for themselves because farming is a very productive sector. Canadian grain farmers are among the most productive, competitive and, indeed, low-cost producers in the world. If they were ever able to achieve the famous level playing field, they would do quite well without any government assistance. All of us in this House, all Canadian taxpayers and all Canadian producers would be very pleased with that but, unfortunately, it is somewhat like Saddam Hussein, it is not possible to wish him away and it is not possible to wish away these harmful international subsidies at the present time.
Last year this government put forward some $500 million in a special income assistance program. Last fall it announced the Cash Flow Enhancement Program which gave farmers access to advances on their farm storage production interest free. This resulted in about $1.5 billion of cash flow being available.
In addition to these programs, the government, through the Farm Debt Review Process, has assisted a number of farmers in resolving difficulties with their creditors. The Farm Credit Corporation has, through various measures, written off enormous amounts of money. There is the Equity Building Program which is assisting a number of Farm Credit Corporation clients who are experiencing difficulty in an attempt to enable them to build up some equity and to re-establish their farming operations. The other side of it, the Canadian Rural Transition Program, has provided income training and assistance to more than 3,500 farm families.
There is another item, a not inconsiderable item, which was perhaps missed in the middle of the GST debate. The implementation of the goods and services tax will relieve the farm community of some $250 million in sales tax on the purchase of their production inputs; a fairly considerable advantage.
There remains a long list of government initiatives towards the grains and oilseeds sector and, indeed, towards other aspects of agriculture, but I am particularly addressing my remarks today to the grains and oilseeds sector. In fact, during the late 1980s federal and provincial governments contributed significantly to farm in-
Supply
come. Direct program payments in fact accounted for 84 per cent of realized net farm income from 1986 to 1989. They more than doubled from an annual average of $1.5 billion during the first half of the 1980s to $3.6 billion for the latter half of that decade. In the prairie provinces where, of course, grain and oilseed production dominates agriculture, the federal share of support averages 86 per cent.
These various ad hoc programs I have outlined were certainly needed, but they show that there were gaps in the safety net program which made it impossible for farmers to be able to predict their incomes. Farmers need some predictability to be able to remain efficient and competitive. That was one of the reasons why, back in 1989, the Minister of Agriculture and this government launched the most comprehensive review of agrifood policies and programs ever undertaken in the history of Canadian agriculture, and did so, I might add, in partnership with the provinces and with the various participants in the agrifood industry.
Through this policy review, the government has attempted to move away from inefficient ad hoc assistance toward a more comprehensive support structure that is fair, cost-efficient and predictable.
For over a year, federal and provincial governments and representatives of the industry have been working in partnership toward this goal. Together there has been undertaken an historic review of agricultural policies and programs. Through the 11 task forces created under the review many Canadians have worked very hard at putting aside their differences to develop solutions for the good of the agricultural industry.
Nowhere, Mr. Speaker, was this more evident than through the work of the grain and oilseeds safety net committee. This federal-provincial-industry committee was established in the early part of 1990 and had something in the order of 34 members of whom 19 were actual hands on farmers, hands on producers. They were able to bring forward a series of recommendations which have resulted in the farm income protection plan legislation which is in front of the House right now, as I mentioned, and indeed the Minister of Agriculture is in front of the agricultural committee right now dealing with aspects of that bill.

March 18, 1991
Supply
GRIP and NISA were developed from the ground up by farmers working with government. Together they have developed a program which provides farmers with predictable support.
At the agrifood policy conference a couple of years ago, farmers indicated that they wanted new safety net programs that would be targeted more effectively to their own individual situations, to their individual operations. They wanted government to take a whole farm approach, they want a predictable support, and these new programs I believe meet these criteria.
The Gross Revenue Insurance Plan and the Net Income Stabilization Account will deal more effectively than any previous programs with the market and production instabilities that farmers have to deal with. The government has put the development of these programs on a fast track because we know that farmers cannot wait, farmers are asking for a new program and the government has responded by creating the environment in which these new programs can be developed.
Mr. Speaker, under current market conditions we anticipate GRIP to pay out approximately $2.7 billion in 1991-92. The establishment of this program will, therefore, ensure a secure underpinning for the future of the grain and oilseeds sector.
GRIP is a reality, Mr. Speaker. Most provinces have agreed to participate and the federal and provincial ministers of agriculture recently agreed on the formula to establish premium rates. It is a very important program, an insurance program whereby the federal government, the provinces and the individual producers contribute toward the premium. It is individualized, it is based on the production of the individual, not of others.
The second component of the safety net program is the Net Income Stabilization Account, or NISA, a cash stabilization account under which farmers are able to contribute up to 2 per cent of their net eligible sales and will receive matching funds from governments whenever the program formula triggers a withdrawal from the fund. It is important to stress here, Mr. Speaker, that each individual producer in the country will have his or her individual NISA account. The individual will control his or her destiny.
We also recognize that GRIP and NISA will not solve all our programs. It is quite clear that no one is going to get rich on these programs. I believe that what they represent today is an important survival mechanism in the face of an extremely difficult world situation.
A government industry committee was established in February to study options to the grains and oilseeds sector. They build on the objectives of GRIP and NISA and deal with issues such as income shortfall, debt burdens, restructuring, land use, the need for adjustment diversification and so on.
The first line of defence is the farmer's responsibility to manage risk as has been stated before in this debate. Stabilization and safety net programs like GRIP and NISA form the second line of defence. There will be no effective third line of defence without a strong second line in place. That is where the third line involves all of us; federal and provincial governments, and producers alike working together to put in place some solutions that will ensure long-term viability.
That means exploring a series of options that will allow us to deal with long-term difficulties in a planned an organized way.
In the recent budget, the government committed an additional $1.3 billion as further proof that we continue to stand by agriculture. This money will be used in part to finance new and ongoing stabilization programs. Some of this money will have to be used to deal with the anticipated deficit in the wheat pool of the Canadian Wheat Board this crop year.
Some of the money will be set aside for special assistance because GRIP and NISA will not pay out until next year. The grains and oilseeds committee, and indeed the horticulture committee are developing options for delivering special assistance. These options will in fact be discussed with farm leaders when the Minister of Agriculture meets with them on Tbesday, two days from now.
An announcement on how special assistance will be delivered is to be made before spring seeding.
In conclusion, I want to stress again that this government has always delivered in terms of support for agriculture. When the farmers need us, we are there. We
March 18, 1991

have responded in the past when they needed assistance, and we are going to continue to do so.

Mr. Speaker, I could not help but notice the member's comment that this government has always delivered in terms of support.
I have a question. I should perhaps go back a little bit. In the summer of 1984 the Minister of Agriculture at the time made a statement that the government was going to seriously support and put in place a program for the development of ethanol blended fuels in Canada. In fact, some research is being done on it at that time.
On August 2, 1984, because we were into a campaign, there was a statement that came from the Progressive Conservative Party that there was a real opportunity for fuel alcohol to be used in Canada as an alternative octane booster in gasoline. The Progressive Conservative Party said that a Progressive Conservative government would set up a special program to encourage the use of alcohol as a lead substitute for octane boosting.
Of course, a few days later, Dr. Gary Gurbin, a former member of this House said: "We would seriously consider mandating the change for environmentally damaging additives to more environmentally acceptable alternatives through federally owned and controlled Crown corporations".
The key is that it is becoming increasingly clear that we have environmental problems that are caused by and as a result of additives in gasoline. We also have great potential in other substances, including both ethanol and methanol.
Of course, on December 2, 1985, the Deputy Minister of Agriculture said: "I support the development of ethanol produced from agricultural resources and forestry products to replace lead as an octane booster for gasoline." He went on.
In May 1986 the Standing Committee on Energy, Mines and Resources reported to this House. The committee recommended the use of methanol and ethanol as blending agents in Canadian gasoline. It recommended that the federal government move more extensively toward research, development and demonstration required to introduce alcohol and gasoline blends on a broader basis and that the federal govem-
Supply
ment co-operate with the provincial governments and industry to establish guidelines and standards for ethanol based fuels.
Does it not make a lot of sense with the low price of grain in the world today to divert a lot of that grain into renewable fuels that are environmentally friendly by the government's own admissions, going back those years, to utilize that grain in Canada in a way that would improve not only the environment but the income to the farmers. It would provide a high protein based livestock feed for the Canadian livestock producers and give them a step up on a lot of the competition. If it was not used for livestock feed, this product could be dried and used as a flour for the manufacture of bread, cookies or biscuits. This particular product is exceptionally well suited for the starving people in Third World countries.
I cannot understand why the government is delaying on this matter. Recent cost studies show that ethanol can be produced for 27 cents a litre. A Canadian company made that statement. Also, in the United States the most economical process can produce it for 38 cents a gallon, with the average price being 47 cents.
I would like to have the comments of the previous speaker as to why the government is delaying on this issue when it can create a market for between 5 million and 8 million bushels of Canadian produced grain in this country.
Mr. Wilson (Swift Current-Maple Creek-Assini-boia: Mr. Speaker, I commend the hon. member for Lambton-Middlesex for what I perceive to be a constructive suggestion. I find it very refreshing and that is why I commend him. Frankly, to this moment I have been rather disappointed by the lack and indeed the almost complete absence of any constructive and concrete suggestions on the part of the opposition. They bring forward a motion, but not much in the way of suggestion, just the usual form of criticism. If I may say, it is sometimes a little hard to swallow, given that the motion emanates from a party whose only legacy to prairie agriculture and western agriculture over the 16-year period from 1968 to 1984 was the LIFT program and the imposition of the capital gains tax.
Perhaps I should add a legacy in the form of approximately a $207 billion national debt as of March 31, 1985, the interest burden of which is the single most significant constraining factor on any government today to be able

March 18, 1991
Supply
to respond adequately to the needs of sectors of the country, be it agriculture or others.
In any event, I do appreciate the hon. member's interest in ethanol. Indeed, while I am far from being an expert, I understand that in fact there have been several initiatives taken under the Western Diversification initiative. I am certainly going to check that out and I will be in touch with the hon. member.
It is important, because his suggestion ties in with one of the three measures I outlined in my remarks that could certainly assist western agriculture, and that was diversification. Diversification within agriculture itself, but also diversification on the prairies but outside of agriculture.
If I may cite an example within my home town of Swift Current which, as an aside, was cited last week by one of the national magazines as one of the 10 most desirable places in the country in which to live. I guess it is that way because, as the magazine indicated, the community spirit and the fairly low cost of housing, low taxes and easy access to a number of amenities.
The one thing we lack in a prairie city which is so dependent on agriculture is a payroll base, a job base. That is where Western Diversification has been helpful. Through Western Diversification and some help from the provincial government, but especially through the initiative of some innovative people, there has been establish an operation impact packaging which will take waste paper and recycle it into environmentally friendly degradable trays for the display of produce. The result is that there will be 135 jobs commencing this summer in this manufacturing plant, absolutely and totally unrelated to agriculture.
In addition, there has already been a spin-off company formed which will employ another 15 constituents in the manufacturing of a coating which will go on the product made by the impact packaging plant.
At a time like this, 150 jobs in a city of some 16,000 people is extremely important. What it means is payroll, it means a spin-off that is unrelated to agriculture. It means, in fact, that some people in the agriculture community who have been relying on straight grain
farming will in fact be able to supplement their incomes through the obtaining of jobs in enterprises such as the one I have described, or in others which are being put forward through the innovative results of the Western Diversification program, a $1.2 billion program which makes repayable loans to enterprises which have new product, new market, new technology, that are seeking to replace imported goods.
I agree very much with the hon. member when he speaks in terms of diversification. I think any measures that can be taken which will lead to diversification of the areas that are so dependent on agriculture are most welcome.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to take part in this opposition day debate at this point. At the onset I will just speak for a moment about some comments made by the minister this morning. When he said there is a 39 per cent net increase in farm income, this is realized farm income.
I should just go back a little bit and point out that during the years 1984-89, the average farm net income increased by only 11 per cent. In 1984-89 the average income of all Canadian families increased by 39 per cent. During this period, due to the lack of farm income, more and more farm families were forced to resort to off-farm income to make ends meet. They had to take jobs off the farm and this level of income, this additional income that came from off farm jobs, increased by 34 per cent.
In spite of those statements, we still have to face reality and realize this government has allowed the people of rural Canada to fall even further behind the rest of society and forced them to take off-farm jobs in order to subsidize their farm operations to grow food for the people of this nation.
On page 9 of the Farm Income Financial Conditions, government expenditures data book, January 1991 you can find these figures. I just want to put that on the record because more and more people are coming to me who are in financial difficulty, people from the riding of Lambton-Middlesex, which is a very large and diversified base of agriculture production.
I have a letter here from four diversified tobacco farmers who are trying to stay afloat. They explain that they are a group of farmers who produce hydroponic lettuce year round. They tell me their product is pesti-
March 18, 1991

cide free, it is clean, and with the roots intact with moisture, it has a much superior shelf life. I should point out that there is no need to spray this kind of lettuce to keep it fresh on the supermarket shelf. They also advise me that they have five family farms producing their product for the past five years, with private money.
It has taken a lot of determination to produce their unique product and to put together a workable marketing plan which, they tell me, is working well. However, it is becoming increasingly difficult for them to compete with American lettuce, mainly from California, that is being dumped into the Ontario market at prices which, questionably, may or may not cover transportation costs.
I will go on and read the rest of the letter:
We feel that we are victimized by American subsidization and policies of their produce. We are aware of their irrigation equipment grants, illegal Mexican labour and large corporate incentives, just to mention a few advantages that we, as Canadians, do not have access to. Free trade has also enhanced dumping procedures.
It does not stop there. These big American dealers, with their government money, have obtained methods to encourage major buyers here to always buy American first. As Canadians, are we put into the back seat of our own market? The major buyers in Canada, in general, feel that they cannot be bothered any more by buying from the family farm in Canada.
Our costs to produce our product is determined by materials, labour and other activities that are generated right here in Canada. If we had the same national privileges as the Americans do, we would be more stable in the marketplace.
We want fair action from our government to make the produce marketplace a fair place to deal. If we are at the woes of the Americans all the time then we are headed for a broke country. We cannot pay enough taxes if we cannot produce enough money to pay them.
That is the end of the quote from this letter. I think it tells it all.
Another of my constituents, or close by to the constituency, is a tobacco grower as well. He calculated that his crop, about 90,000 pounds of tobacco, will translate into roughly $9 million revenue for two levels of government this year at the federal level and the provincial level. In 1990 Ontario tobacco growers sold a total of $123.2 million pounds to Canada's big three cigarette manufacturers, worth $181.1 million or $1.47 pound. In 1989 cash receipts added up to $261.1 million. Between them, the federal and provincial governments collect more than $5 billion a year in revenue from tobacco products.

When we look at the revenue income from tobacco products and distilled products in this country, they take in billions upon billions of dollars from that primary producer of this nation and yet, at the same time, this government brags about handing out $1.3 billion to the Canadian farmers to help bail them out of trouble, bailing out the people who lay the golden egg in terms of the department of revenue of this nation.
I cannot help but look back at two years ago now when on the floor of this House I asked the Minister of Agriculture about the no-rolled beef being imported into this country, a million pounds a week at that time. He assured me that he would look into it, but the closure of six packing plants since 1989 is due in part to the government's inaction on no-rolled beef being allowed to come into Canada from the United States.
One of these packing plants has re-opened, but the fact is that the amount of no-rolled beef-a cheap product coming into this country from the United States, most of it dairy cows that have been slaughtered over there after one or two lactations-coming into this country which is not graded, and that is why it is called no-rolled. When you grade a carcass of beef in the slaughterhouse, you run a roll down the side and it tells you whether it is A-l, A-2, A-3 or A-4. If it is cow beef, they call it C-l, C-2, C-3 or C-4. All this is coming in here and the consumers do not know what they are buying. The amount of that has tripled since 1989. The feedlot industry across this province has been decimated.
Yesterday, in The Ottawa Citizen there was a story about Ontario's once powerful beef industry taking it on the chin. It is having an impact on our environment, it is having an impact on the income of this country and it is taking away jobs. We have to look to our food processing industry in this nation, whether it is the beef packing industry, the lettuce producers, to see what is happening to this country under this government in allowing imports of products from other countries. While we cannot export beef that is not graded, we are letting it into this country. I ask the government to do something about it, to put a stable foundation under the beef industry in this country so that we know precisely where we stand and what lies ahead of us.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to rise today to address the motion before the House imploring and encouraging the government to take some immediate action to assist primary producers in this country to get over the hurdle facing them as a result of the disastrous prices in 1990-1991.
I will refer first to the situation of grain farmers in western Canada who went through several years of drought. They did not have anything to sell. I would like to draw a little comparison. That is like someone else in the rest of Canada having to sit down at the dinner table every night and saying to the family: "I am sorry, folks, I still don't have a job so we don't have an income", because they just did not have anything to sell, there was nothing in the bin.
If we follow on to what happened in 1990, they got a job or they got an excellent crop. They did. They had an excellent crop, pretty well evenly spread, although there were pockets where it was no so good. That always happens when dealing with mother nature. But they got that crop and because of what is going on in the world in trade wars it was not worth anything. Basically they had a job but they still were not getting a pay cheque.
That is the conundrum they are in at this time of year. They need money to get them through.
We met with the prairie pools the other day. There is talk, I agree, good talk; I just came from a committee meeting in which we were talking about the GRIP and NISA programs. They are not going to kick in for the 1990-1991 crop year. They can and will kick in down the road, but they are not going to provide that bridge financing for the 1990-1991 crop year. That assistance is definitely needed.
The Western Grain Stabilization Act will put some money in there, but the prairie pools tell us that to bring them up even close to the average net farm income they had in the last number of years they need $1.1 billion or $1.16 billion; somewhere in that neighbourhood, a considerable sum of money.
I know money is not easy to come by, and I am not here to say to the government: spend, spend, spend. What I know, what those of us in the agrifood industry know, and what we should all realize as Canadians is that every dollar that arrives at the farm gate will multiply seven times before it is through our economy and our society. That is a lot of money when it goes through.
One out of five Canadian jobs results from what happens at the primary producer level. One out of five Canadian jobs is in the agrifood industry. It is important that that sector of our economy, that sector of our business world in this country, is kept sound. What we are asking the government to do today is to react, to realize that and to do something now.
I wish I did not have to stand here and ask this today, to discuss this with the government, to debate this in the House of Commons, but it is a reality of where we are as a result of what happened in 1990.
I would like to give some examples of what is happening in the horticultural industry as well. In discussions about the agrifood industry we hear about third line of defence, second line of defence, and working back to first line of defence. What I can say and what I am hearing is that there is nothing wrong. There are some good things with the second line of defence, such as the GRIP and NISA programs and the Farm Income Stabilization Act which takes into account the hopefully not needed necessity of a third line of defence. The government also has to move quickly, and quite frankly in some cases has to move, on the first line of defence. That first line of defence talks about border inspection, grade standards, equalizing and levelling the playing field for such things as crop production requirements, be they chemicals or whatever, with our major competitor in the horticultural field, the United States.
The horticultural industry in Canada is a $2.2 billion industry itself and $500 million of that is exported. It is important that our players, our producers, be on an equal playing field and equal footing with those they are competing against.

March 18, 1991

The Minister of State for Grains and Oilseeds stated last week that action had to be taken within six weeks. One of those weeks is gone already, and we have not seen the action. I just saying that the producers need to know. Producers are looking at a longer term situation, but right now their bankers are saying to them: "What are we going to look at and what is there so that we can get to the 1991 crop?"
Some very startling things are happening out there. In my own riding a food processing facility announced about six weeks ago that it was no longer going to process food.
I heard the minister stand last week and say that a number of new food processing facilities are being constructed in this country in the last number of months.
I spoke as recently as this morning with the chief executive officer of a major food processing company, and his answer was: "I am in the industry, and I do not know where they are. If we have got new food processing facilities, they must be hamburger and fast food outlets in the city some place". He did not know where they were.
When they pulled out of processing tomatoes, pumpkins and peas in my riding in Prince Edward County, it took out $1.3 million from farm gate prices. If we multiply that by five, six, seven or whatever figure we want, we find that is a tremendous removal of funds from there and the employment that went with it. The chief executive office also said to me this morning: "The rules are changed. The tariffs are changing. We have globalization," et cetera. His answer to me was: "Mr. Vanclief, it is cheaper to buy it south of the border".
I understand that those business decisions have to be made. I am asking the government: What does it suggest that these producers turn to in order to make their living? The neat answer is: "You have lost your job because of competitiveness", but what will the government put in place to allow these people to make a living? What is the government going to put in place immediately to provide the producers who are still there with a financially sound basis in order to get through the disastrous results of the 1990 crop year?
I cannot say it enough: A bridging type of program is needed. Horticultural producers in the province of Ontario have worked their figures. They claim that they need $70 million to get them even close to where they have been on the average in the past number of years. That is one province.

I know all provinces in the horticultural industry were not affected in the same way. British Columbia has been affected, as has the maritimes, but they agree that the main hurt this year have been in the province of Ontario.
I ask the government to react to this as quickly as it possibly can so that producers know where they are at for 1991.1 will leave it at that, Mr. Speaker, and there may be some comments.

Mr. Speaker, I would just like to make a comment.

There has never been a government in the history of this country that has stood with the farmers like the Conservative government, the Prime Minister, and the Minister of Agriculture. There has been strong representation throughout the grains and oilseeds industry, horticulture and agriculture as a whole.

I am not saying that is enough, nor that it has solved all the problems, but certainly if there has ever been a government that has been sensitive to the need, it is this government.
What about the present situation? This past winter the Minister of Agriculture called together farm groups from across the country: 19 farm groups, all the wheat pools, all wheat growers. All the organizations were represented. Farmers themselves, with support from the federal government and the provincial governments, brought together programs that are now called GRIP and NISA. They are being well accepted.
I just want to assure the opposition and our farmers out there that if ever there has been a government that will stand with them, this government will, has, and will continue to.
The importance of the strength of this government is that we represent all the regions of this country. We represent Quebec, Ontario, the west, the maritimes, and right across the country. One important point our farmers are making is that it is important this country

stay together as a strong federation so that we can continue to do what has been done in the past: support agriculture. I just want to make the point that our government has stood with the farmers, will continue to stand with them, and these programs will work in the future.

Mr. Speaker, I do not quarrel with some of the comments of my friend across the floor about the dollars that have been put into agriculture. What he did not address is the subject matter of the motion today.
He talked about what he has done in the past. He talked about what he hopes to do in the future. But fanners want to know what he is going to do now.
The programs and the action taken for the 1989 crop year are not going to take place again. We are talking constructively. We are talking about what will happen or what can happen for 1991 on. However there is a gap or a bridging in there, and we are asking the government what it is going to do.
Today the Minister of Finance says the money is not available, the $1.3 billion increase in the agriculture budget this year is used up for the Canadian Wheat Board for western grain stabilization. He says the money is not available.
